relevant_group_routes.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Governmentality: Foucault's 'Governmentality', Gordon, Burchell and Rose anthologised in his Class (1995); The Rule of Freedom 'develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography' (2003); governmentality as 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable', though prone to 'crypto-functionalism' (2014)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words: 'History and Governmentality' (2014, read in full), quoting Rose: governmentality 'concerns the ways in which those who would exercise rule have posed to themselves the question' of how to govern; 'a kind of intellectual machinery or apparatus for rendering reality thinkable'; governmentality studies 'suffered also from a tendency to a sort of crypto-functionalism'; 'In developing the work of Foucault alongside the new materialism, I and my recent collaborator Chandra Mukerji begin from the assertion' that modern states are impersonal social formations. BJS 2010 (opening read) reprises Rose and Miller. Verso description of The Rule of Freedom (read): 'creatively and originally develops Foucauldian approaches to historiography'. Class (1995) contents: Foucault's 'Governmentality' (pp. 201–203), Gordon and Burchell, Donzelot, Rose. Koditschek (2014, read): The State of Freedom 'draws largely on the ideas of Michel Foucault'.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Credits Gerstle’s intellectual and editorial interventions with improving Impossible Subjects.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The acknowledgment, p. xvii, singles out Gerstle while also crediting series editors William Chafe, Linda Gordon and Julian Zelizer. The 1999 author note acknowledges his support and constructive criticism; the 2014 foreword, note 4, lists American Crucible among resources on racial history. Other editors' contributions are not assigned to him, and editorial assistance is not formal supervision. His original books remain unread.
